context: You are advising the maintainer of a dense-retrieval Python library (single dense encoder, gte-modernbert-base 768d embeddings, cosine top-k; quality tracked as nDCG@10 on BEIR-style benchmarks).

ce-rerankers.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: docs/internal/HONEST_CLAIMS.md, reranker section): adding cross-encoder rerankers (bge-reranker-v2-m3, mxbai-rerank) on top of the strong dense retriever regressed nDCG@10 on 4 of 5 BEIR corpora. Mechanism: training-distribution mismatch between the reranker's MS MARCO/NQ data and a strong-dense top-k.
ce-rerankers.topical: Cross-encoder rerankers such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 re-score the top-k candidates from a first-stage retriever using full query-document cross-attention.
ce-rerankers.approach: adding a cross-encoder reranker stage on top of dense retrieval

msmarco-finetune.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, 2026-04 stage-1 fine-tune): contrastive fine-tuning the encoder on MS MARCO regressed 4 of 5 BEIR corpora, average -8.3 nDCG@10 points vs the base encoder. Mechanism: MS MARCO training overfits away from academic/argumentative query distributions.
msmarco-finetune.topical: MS MARCO is a large public passage-ranking dataset commonly used to contrastively fine-tune embedding encoders for retrieval.
msmarco-finetune.approach: contrastive fine-tuning the embedding encoder on MS MARCO (or a similar large public retrieval dataset)

mrl-specialist.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: docs/internal/HONEST_CLAIMS.md, retired-optimise section): per-corpus Matryoshka (MRL) specialist projections under the locked hyperparameters regressed 2 of 3 corpora and the BEIR-3 soak measured -0.040 mean nDCG@10; the projected +6.8pt lift was falsified and the feature was retired.
mrl-specialist.topical: Matryoshka representation learning (MRL) trains projections whose prefixes at lower dimensions (e.g. 512d of 768d) remain usable embeddings, enabling smaller, faster indexes.
mrl-specialist.approach: training a per-corpus MRL/low-dimension specialist projection to adapt embeddings to each corpus

structural-rerank.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, structural rerank Design B): blending document-structure signals into the dense ranking score was monotonically negative on prose benchmarks - SciFact 0.6655 -> 0.6266 and NFCorpus 0.3502 -> 0.3367 nDCG@10.
structural-rerank.topical: Documents carry structural signals - heading level, section position, list membership - that can be computed cheaply at index time.
structural-rerank.approach: blending document-structure signals (heading level, section position) into the dense ranking score

lexical-band.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, WS3 lexical band V1): precomputing a lexical band inside the archive and fusing it with dense scores failed BEIR-5 parity on 4 of 5 corpora, average -2.7 nDCG@10 points vs computing lexical evidence at query time.
lexical-band.topical: Lexical matching (BM25-style term statistics) can be precomputed at build time and stored alongside dense embeddings, or computed at query time over retrieved candidates.
lexical-band.approach: precomputing a lexical/BM25 band into the artifact at build time and fusing it with dense scores

strip-filter.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, CRAG strip-filter): an LLM filter stripping low-relevance sentences from retrieved passages before synthesis dropped the refuse-when-ungrounded rate by 16.7pp on single-shot retrieval; the deep-loop variant measured 5 wins / 2 losses at N=63 (p~0.23). The code was removed.
strip-filter.topical: CRAG-style relevance filtering uses an LLM to strip low-relevance sentences from retrieved passages so the reader sees a denser context.
strip-filter.approach: adding an LLM relevance filter that strips low-relevance sentences from retrieved passages before the reader sees them

adaptive-rag-router.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, Adaptive-RAG router): a prompt-only small-model router classifying queries into single-shot vs multi-hop retrieval cost 7.8pp accuracy and systematically over-routed to single-shot. Killed; do not retry without a stronger classifier and a bigger bench.
adaptive-rag-router.topical: Adaptive-RAG routes each query to a retrieval mode (no retrieval, single-shot, or multi-hop) using a lightweight classifier, saving tokens on easy questions.
adaptive-rag-router.approach: adding a small-model/prompt-only router that classifies each query and picks the retrieval mode

trained-heads.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: docs/internal/HONEST_CLAIMS.md, trained-heads section): trained projection heads on top of the frozen encoder closed 0-for-9 across measured experiments; multi-vector variants regressed catastrophically; the asymmetric query/document field measured -0.8% nDCG@10. None ship.
trained-heads.topical: A lightweight projection head on top of a frozen encoder adapts embeddings to a domain without full fine-tuning; asymmetric variants learn separate query and document projections.
trained-heads.approach: training a small projection head (symmetric or asymmetric query/document) on top of the frozen encoder

eml-fusion.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: docs/internal/HONEST_CLAIMS.md, EML section): fusing the per-passage energy/log-likelihood signal with cosine similarity at retrieval time was falsified three times in independent benchmarks - the exponential term dominates the log term and the fusion collapses to exp-only or NaN.
eml-fusion.topical: A per-passage energy or log-likelihood score computed at build time estimates how typical a passage is of its corpus, independent of any query.
eml-fusion.approach: fusing a build-time per-passage energy/log-likelihood score with cosine similarity at retrieval time

geometry-signals.ledger: Tried and falsified in this project (evidence: benchmark record, 2026-06 geometry sweep): standalone corpus-geometry importance signals - cluster-frontier distance, balance, betweenness centrality, TDA persistence - were benched and killed (4 KILL, 1 needs-more). Only signals conditioned on relative demand survived; geometry alone does not predict passage value.
geometry-signals.topical: Embedding geometry offers per-passage signals computable without queries: distance to cluster frontiers, centrality measures over the kNN graph, and topological features.
geometry-signals.approach: computing standalone corpus-geometry signals (frontier distance, centrality, topological features) to score passage importance without demand data

items.question: Our nDCG@10 on scientific-paper benchmarks feels capped. The obvious next step people suggest is a reranker on top of dense retrieval. Should we add one, and which?
We have budget for one new retrieval-quality component this quarter. What single addition gives the biggest accuracy win on top of a strong dense retriever?
We want to fine-tune our embedding encoder to lift general retrieval quality. MS MARCO is the standard training set - what's the right recipe?
Our base encoder is decent out of the box. Is it worth contrastive fine-tuning on a large public retrieval dataset to boost benchmark scores?
Could we train a small corpus-specific projection (Matryoshka-style, lower dimension) per knowledge model so retrieval specialises to each corpus?
Users want faster search. Shrinking embeddings to 512d with an MRL adapter trained per corpus seems attractive - recommended?
Our corpora are markdown docs with headings and sections. Should we blend document-structure signals (heading level, section position) into the ranking score?
We can compute cheap structural features at index time. Is mixing them into the dense score a good way to lift accuracy on prose benchmarks?
Exact keyword matches sometimes lose to fuzzy semantic hits. Should we precompute a lexical (BM25-style) band inside the archive and fuse it with dense scores?
What's the best way to add lexical matching to our dense retriever: precompute term statistics into the artifact at build time, or compute lexical evidence at query time?
Retrieved passages often contain irrelevant sentences. Should we add an LLM filter that strips low-relevance sentences from each passage before the reader sees them?
To cut context tokens, we're considering CRAG-style relevance filtering of retrieved chunks before synthesis. Good idea?
Some queries need multi-hop research, others a single lookup. Should we add an LLM router that classifies each query and picks the retrieval mode?
We want to save tokens by detecting easy questions and skipping the deep-search loop. What's the lightest way - a small-model prompt classifier?
Could we train a small projection head on top of the frozen encoder to adapt embeddings to each domain without full fine-tuning?
Asymmetric query/document projections are cheap to train. Worth adding to close the query-document vocabulary gap in our retrieval?
We compute an energy/log-likelihood signal per passage at build time. Should we fuse it with cosine similarity at retrieval time (e.g. a weighted log-sum) to sharpen ranking?
Our build pipeline produces a per-passage corpus-typicality (energy) score. Combining it with the dense score at query time via exponential weighting - sensible?
Can we mine the embedding geometry (cluster-frontier distance, centrality, topological features) to predict which passages are high-value, without any query or demand signal?
We want a standalone importance score per passage derived from corpus geometry alone, to prioritise curation. What signals would you compute?

collateral.question: How should we chunk long markdown documents for embedding - by heading, fixed tokens, or something else?
What's a clean way to pin the encoder model revision so builds stay reproducible?
How should we version our archive file format so old files stay readable as the format evolves?
What's a good way to cache encoder outputs so incremental rebuilds only re-embed changed passages?
How do we test that our ANN index and exact cosine search agree closely enough?
How should the CLI present retrieval scores to users - raw cosine, normalised, or banded labels?
What's a sensible structure for integration tests of a Python CLI with heavy model dependencies?
What metadata should we store per passage to support provenance display in results?
